subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]
passage: Aparna here. Harsha, who sits opposite me at the design studio, told me over lunch what he had done. "I paid for three months at the gym, all at once," he said. "I know myself. If I pay month to month, I'll skip and tell myself I'll pay next time. But money already gone will make me feel silly for not going." He said it like a rule he had checked. The first week I saw his gym bag under the desk every morning. On day nine it stayed on the chair and he left at six sharp. I don't know if he enjoys it or just doesn't want to waste the money. When I asked, he shrugged and said, "Either is fine with me."

qa.q: How many months did Harsha pay for?
qa.a: Harsha paid for three months, all at once.

qa.q: What did Harsha expect from paying everything at once?
qa.a: Harsha expected that money already gone would make him feel silly for skipping, so he would go.

qa.q: What could Harsha do if he still skips despite having paid?
qa.a: Harsha could add a workout partner or fixed times in his calendar, since the payment alone may not be enough.

qa.q: Why can Aparna not say whether Harsha enjoys the gym?
qa.a: Aparna only sees the bag and Harsha leaving at six, and Harsha said either reason was fine.

grounding: Shows a worker paying for a three-month plan upfront, expecting money already spent to make him attend.

subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]
passage:
Week 1: Hrithik stood at the gym counter in Pune, holding his phone. Monthly plan or three months upfront? He thought it through. "Last year I paid monthly and quit in week three, because stopping cost me nothing. If I pay for three months now, skipping means wasting money I already spent. I hate wasting money." He paid for three months. His friend Tanvir raised an eyebrow.

Week 5: Rain, a late night at work, and a strong urge to skip. Hrithik looked at the receipt on his fridge. "Already paid for this morning." He went, grumbling.

Week 12: Tanvir asked if he'd renew. Hrithik shrugged. "Maybe monthly now. Going is just what I do in the morning."

qa.q: What did Hrithik stick on his fridge?
qa.a: The receipt for the three-month plan.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling in week 5, and what kept him going?
qa.a: He felt tired and tempted to skip, but hated the idea of wasting money he had already spent.

qa.q: Why might paying upfront have worked for Hrithik this time?
qa.a: It made quitting feel costly, so he kept going long enough for the habit to form; by week 12 he didn't need the push.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Hrithik's choice at the start?
qa.a: Tanvir seems doubtful, raising an eyebrow, perhaps expecting Hrithik to quit again.

grounding: A young worker pays for a three-month gym plan upfront, knowing money already spent will make him more likely to go.

subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]
passage: Siami, you asked how I kept at the gym all these years. When I was twenty-four and new at the post office in Aizawl, I tried three times and quit three times. Each time I paid by the month, and each time the first bad weather stopped me. So I sat down and thought: what will stop your Lokesh Uncle from quitting? I knew myself. I hate losing money more than I hate cold mornings. So I paid for three whole months, all at once, and told my friends. On the wet, grey mornings, I lay in bed and thought, "That money is already gone. If you stay here, you're throwing it away." And up I got. After three months, I didn't need the trick.

qa.q: How old was Lokesh when he started at the post office?
qa.a: Lokesh was twenty-four and new at the post office in Aizawl.

qa.q: What did young Lokesh feel on the wet, grey mornings?
qa.a: Young Lokesh felt reluctant and tempted to stay in bed, but the thought of wasting the money pushed him up.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Paying for three months at once, because he knew he hated losing money more than cold mornings, so quitting now had a cost.

qa.q: How might young Lokesh's friends have seen his plan?
qa.a: They probably found it funny, but knowing they'd heard about it may have added to his wish not to quit.

grounding: An elder recalls paying for three months of gym upfront so that money already spent would make him more likely to attend.
